content.summary: Read a short work email about a project update. Notice how the writer makes requests politely, refers to an earlier conversation, and closes the message in a professional way. You will practise finding the main idea and important details in a business email.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use could and would to make polite requests, and may to ask permission. After could and may, use the base form of the verb. After would you mind, use a verb ending in -ing.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn common phrases for following up, referring to a topic, mentioning an attachment, making a polite request, and closing an email.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: First skim the email to understand its purpose. Then scan it for names, dates, requested actions, and information about attached files.

learningObjectives: Understand the main purpose of a short professional email.
Find specific details about a deadline, an attachment, and the action requested.
Recognize polite request patterns with could, would, and may.
Identify common phrases used to open and close business emails.

contextWarmup.prompt: You need a colleague to send you a project file. Which message sounds polite and professional?
options: Could you please send me the project file when you have a moment?
contextWarmup.explanation: Could you please makes the request polite. The other options sound too direct for many workplace situations.

rules: Use could you plus the base form of a verb for a polite request: Could you send the report?
Use would you mind plus a verb ending in -ing for a very polite request: Would you mind checking the figures?
Use may I plus the base form of a verb to ask permission: May I suggest another date?

commonTrap.explanation: After would you mind, use a verb ending in -ing. Do not use the base form directly after mind.
commonTrap.wrong: Would you mind send me the notes?
commonTrap.correct: Would you mind sending me the notes?

content.passageTitle: A Follow-up About the Project Plan
paragraphs:
Subject: Follow-up regarding the project plan

Dear Daniel,

I am writing to follow up on our conversation about the training project last Tuesday. I have attached the revised plan, including the new schedule and the estimated costs. Could you please review the dates and confirm that they work for your team by Thursday afternoon?

Would you mind checking the cost section as well? I would appreciate it if you could send me any changes before our meeting on Friday. If the new schedule is difficult, may I suggest moving the first training session to 18 June? Please let me know what you think at your earliest convenience.

I look forward to hearing from you. Thank you for your time and help.

Kind regards,
Maya

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Polite and Professional Emails

content.summary: A professional email has a clear subject, a polite greeting, a brief reason for writing, and a suitable closing. Use polite request forms such as could, would, and may. Keep each paragraph focused, and check names, punctuation, and verb forms before sending.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Open with a Clear Greeting
blueprintItems.formula: Dear + name / Hello + name, then a brief opening sentence
blueprintItems.example: Dear Ms Patel, I hope you are well.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Make a Tactful Request
blueprintItems.formula: Could you + base verb + please? / Would you mind + verb-ing?
blueprintItems.example: Could you please check the attached report? Would you mind sharing your comments?

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Close Politely
blueprintItems.formula: I would appreciate it if you could + base verb. + Thank you / Kind regards
blueprintItems.example: I would appreciate it if you could reply by Thursday. Thank you for your help. Kind regards, Alex

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after a greeting and after a closing phrase.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Dear Mr Lee I am writing about the schedule.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Dear Mr Lee, I am writing about the schedule.
mechanicsRules.why: The comma separates the greeting from the message.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a base verb after could, may, and would in request formulas.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Could you please to review this file?
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Could you please review this file?
mechanicsRules.why: These modal verbs are followed by the base form of the verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a verb ending in -ing after Would you mind.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Would you mind to send the agenda?
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Would you mind sending the agenda?
mechanicsRules.why: The phrase Would you mind is followed by a verb ending in -ing.

content.summary: Practise speaking clearly and politely about professional emails. Use could, would, and may to make requests sound considerate. Stress key information, such as the action you need and the deadline.
content.audioGuidance: Speak at a steady pace and finish each thought clearly. Use a gentle rising intonation for polite questions, such as “Could you send the attachment?” Use falling intonation for statements and email closings. Pause briefly between the reason for your request and the request itself.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear vowel sounds in key business words
pillars.explanation: Say the vowel sounds clearly in words such as “email,” “please,” and “regarding.” Avoid rushing through longer words.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.target: Stress the important syllable in longer words
pillars.explanation: Practise words such as “attachment” and “convenience.” Clear word stress helps your listener understand you.

pillars.name: Polite Intonation
pillars.target: Use a gentle rise in polite questions
pillars.explanation: Let your voice rise slightly at the end of questions with “could” or “would.” Keep the tone friendly, not demanding.

pillars.name: Natural Pausing
pillars.explanation: Give the listener time to follow your message. For example, pause after “I’m writing to follow up on our meeting” before making your request.
